Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H_G,H_Q$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and fix
the factor order $H_G\otimes H_Q$. For ordered orthonormal bases
$(g_s)$ and $(q_\alpha)$, define
$$\operatorname{Tr}_G:\mathcal B(H_G\otimes H_Q)\to\mathcal B(H_Q),\qquad (\operatorname{Tr}_G X)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_sX_{(s,\alpha),(s,\beta)},$$
where $X_{(s,\alpha),(t,\beta)}=\langle X(g_t\otimes q_\beta),
g_s\otimes q_\alpha\rangle$ under the linear-first convention. Equivalently,
this is the partial trace over the second factor after swapping the two wires.
The partial-trace characterization and wire-permutation unitarity in
[[thm-qc-partial-trace-characterization-and-basis-independence]] and
[[thm-qc-wire-permutation-is-unitary]] show that the map is independent of
the chosen orthonormal bases. In particular, the same definition applies when
$H_Q=H_L\otimes H_R$, with that residual factor order left unchanged. For an
operator on $(H_G\otimes H_L)\otimes H_R$, use the canonical associator of
the ordered tensor-register construction to view it on
$H_G\otimes(H_L\otimes H_R)$ before taking this partial trace.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a
non-negative operator $R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$,
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$ is non-negative and

$$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R))=\operatorname{tr}(R).$$

Here $\operatorname{End}(H)$ is the set of linear maps $H\to H$ as in
[[def-qc-partial-trace]], $I_H$ denotes the identity map $x\mapsto x$, and both
conclusions include zero-dimensional factors.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

derivations.claim: By the second-factor formula [F2] and the positivity/trace theorem [F4], $\rho_A=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ is non-negative and has trace $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{AB})=1$. It is therefore a density operator by [F1].

Choose ordered orthonormal bases $(a_i)$ and $(b_j)$ of $H_A,H_B$ by [F7]. Formula [F3] and the product inner product in [F6] give $\langle\rho_B y,y\rangle=\sum_i\langle\rho_{AB}(a_i\otimes y),a_i\otimes y\rangle$ for every $y\in H_B$; every summand is nonnegative by [F1] and [F5]. The matrix formula [F3] also shows $\rho_B$ is self-adjoint because $\rho_{AB}$ is self-adjoint. Hence $\rho_B$ is non-negative.

Summing the diagonal entries in [F3] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_B)=\sum_{i,j}(\rho_{AB})_{(i,j),(i,j)}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{AB})=1$ by [F8] and [F1]. Therefore $\rho_B$ is a density operator by [F1].

derivations.claim: Every $v\in H_X\otimes H_B$ has a unique form $v=\sum_{x\in X}\xi_x\otimes v_x$. Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

derivations.claim: All adjoints of the finite-dimensional linear maps used below exist uniquely by [F5]. Let $C$ be positive definite on a finite-dimensional space and $y$ any vector. The operator $C$ is injective by [F3], hence invertible in finite dimension; put $z_0=C^{-1}y$. Expanding with [F1]–[F2] gives $2\operatorname{Re}\langle y,z\rangle-\langle Cz,z\rangle=\langle C^{-1}y,y\rangle-\langle C(z-z_0),z-z_0\rangle$. The last term is nonnegative by [F3] and vanishes at $z=z_0$, so $\langle C^{-1}y,y\rangle=\max_z\{2\operatorname{Re}\langle y,z\rangle-\langle Cz,z\rangle\}$.

If $H=\{0\}$ the assertion is immediate. Otherwise fix $x\in H$, put $C=T+sI_K$ and $y=Vx$. By [F2] and $V^*V=I_H$, $V^*CV=V^*TV+sI_H$, which is positive definite. Restrict the maximum in step 1.1 to $z=Vw$; the isometry identity gives $\langle Vx,Vw\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle$ and $\langle CVw,Vw\rangle=\langle(V^*TV+sI_H)w,w\rangle$. Hence $\langle (T+sI_K)^{-1}Vx,Vx\rangle\ge\langle(V^*TV+sI_H)^{-1}x,x\rangle$. This holds for every $x$, so the self-adjoint operator difference is non-negative by [F4], proving the order inequality.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Set $g(t)=t-1-\ln t$ for $t>0$. Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces. A
**quantum channel** from $H$ to $K$ is a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ ([[def-linear-map]]) that is completely
positive ([[def-qc-completely-positive-map]]) and trace-preserving, meaning

$$\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}(X)\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where trace is the basis-independent trace of a finite-dimensional
endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]). Trace preservation is
required on the full operator space, not only on density operators. This
definition is mathematical and assumes no physical realization.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

$T:V\to V$ be linear. The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is
self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$

for every $v\in V$.

The operator $T$ is **positive** when $T$ is self-adjoint and

$$\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$$

for every nonzero $v\in V$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.

modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either

$$S(A)_\rho:=S(\rho_A),\qquad S(A\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})-S(\rho_B),\qquad I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a finite tripartite state $\rho_{ABC}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, set $\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_{H_C}\rho_{ABC}$ after identifying the factors as $(H_A\otimes H_B)\otimes H_C$, and $\rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_{H_A}\rho_{ABC}$ after identifying them as $H_A\otimes(H_B\otimes H_C)$. $$I(A:B\mid C)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AC})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_C)-S(\rho_{ABC}).$$

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, let $T:K\to K$ be positive definite, and let $V:H\to K$ satisfy $V^*V=I_H$. Then, in the non-negative operator order,

$$-\ln(V^*TV)\preceq V^*(-\ln T)V,$$

where $R\preceq S$ means $S-R$ is non-negative and logarithms of positive-definite operators are defined by finite spectral calculus.

Let $A,B$ be positive-definite operators on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$. On $\mathcal L(H)$, with Hilbert-Schmidt inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle_{\rm HS}:=\operatorname{tr}(XY^*)$, define $\Delta_{B,A}(X):=BXA^{-1}$. Then $\Delta_{B,A}$ is positive definite and

$$D(A\|B)=\langle(-\ln\Delta_{B,A})(A^{1/2}),A^{1/2}\rangle_{\rm HS}.$$

The logarithm of $\Delta_{B,A}$ is defined by its positive eigenvalues.

For non-negative $A,B$ on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space,

$$\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}D(A+\varepsilon I\|B+\varepsilon I)=D(A\|B),$$

where the right side may be $+\infty$ under the support convention of [[def-it-finite-dimensional-quantum-relative-entropy]].

For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$,

$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

The two products may have different sizes, and the equality includes $m=0$ or
$n=0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

derivations.claim: All adjoints of the finite-dimensional linear maps used below exist uniquely by [F8]. Discard all indices with $\lambda_i=0$ from both sides; at least one index remains because the weights sum to one. The remaining weights are strictly positive and still sum to one. If $H=\{0\}$, all operators and relative entropies are zero by [F1], so the result holds. Now assume $H\ne\{0\}$ and first suppose every $A_i,B_i$ is positive definite. Set $A=\sum_i\lambda_iA_i$ and $B=\sum_i\lambda_iB_i$. Positive-definite square roots and inverse square roots exist by [F6]. On the Hilbert-Schmidt spaces, with direct-sum inner product, define $U_i(X):=\sqrt{\lambda_i}XA^{-1/2}A_i^{1/2}$ and $U(X):=(U_i(X))_i$. Trace cyclicity [F5] and the adjoint definition [F7] in $\langle U_i(X),Y\rangle_{\rm HS}$ give $U_i^*(Y)=\sqrt{\lambda_i}YA_i^{1/2}A^{-1/2}$. Therefore $U^*U(X)=XA^{-1/2}(\sum_i\lambda_iA_i)A^{-1/2}=X$, so $U$ is an isometry.

Put $T:=\bigoplus_i\Delta_{B_i,A_i}$, positive definite by [F3]. For each $i$, multiplication gives $U_i^*\Delta_{B_i,A_i}U_i(X)=\lambda_iB_iXA^{-1}$, hence $U^*TU(X)=BXA^{-1}=\Delta_{B,A}(X)$; also $U(A^{1/2})=(\sqrt{\lambda_i}A_i^{1/2})_i$ by [F6]. Apply [F2] to $U,T$ and evaluate the order inequality on $A^{1/2}$ in the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product. Using [F3] on both sides yields $D(A\|B)\le\sum_i\lambda_iD(A_i\|B_i)$.

For general non-negative $A_i,B_i$, if some $D(A_i\|B_i)=+\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the claim holds. Otherwise each $\operatorname{supp}(A_i)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B_i)$. If $v\in\ker B$, where $B=\sum_i\lambda_iB_i$, then $0=\langle Bv,v\rangle=\sum_i\lambda_i\langle B_iv,v\rangle$ forces $B_iv=0$ for every $i$; support inclusion then gives $A_iv=0$, so $Av=0$. Thus $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$. Apply the positive-definite case to $A_i+\varepsilon I,B_i+\varepsilon I$; their weighted sums are $A+\varepsilon I,B+\varepsilon I$. Let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and use [F4] for every term to obtain the desired inequality.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty classical label set, represented by a register $H_X$ with computational orthonormal basis $(\xi_x)_{x\in X}$ ([[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]]). For each $x$, write $\Pi_xz:=\langle z,\xi_x\rangle\xi_x$, the rank-one orthogonal projection using the root linear-first convention, as in [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Let $H_B$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. A finite **classical-quantum state** is

$$\rho_{XB}:=\sum_{x\in X}p_x\Pi_x\otimes\rho_x,$$

where $p_x\ge0$, $\sum_xp_x=1$, and each $\rho_x$ is a density operator on $H_B$. It is a density operator by [[lem-it-finite-cq-block-sum-is-a-state]]. Its quantum marginal is $\bar\rho_B:=\sum_xp_x\rho_x=\operatorname{Tr}_X\rho_{XB}$ by the second-factor partial-trace formula in [[def-qc-partial-trace]], and it is a density operator by [[lem-it-partial-traces-of-a-state-are-states]]. The **Holevo information** of this ensemble is

$$\chi(\{p_x,\rho_x\}_{x\in X}):=S(\bar\rho_B)-\sum_{x:p_x>0}p_xS(\rho_x),$$

where zero-probability branches contribute nothing. This is measured in nats under [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Let $H_G,H_Q$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and fix
the factor order $H_G\otimes H_Q$. For ordered orthonormal bases
$(g_s)$ and $(q_\alpha)$, define
$$\operatorname{Tr}_G:\mathcal B(H_G\otimes H_Q)\to\mathcal B(H_Q),\qquad (\operatorname{Tr}_G X)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_sX_{(s,\alpha),(s,\beta)},$$
where $X_{(s,\alpha),(t,\beta)}=\langle X(g_t\otimes q_\beta),
g_s\otimes q_\alpha\rangle$ under the linear-first convention. Equivalently,
this is the partial trace over the second factor after swapping the two wires.
The partial-trace characterization and wire-permutation unitarity in
[[thm-qc-partial-trace-characterization-and-basis-independence]] and
[[thm-qc-wire-permutation-is-unitary]] show that the map is independent of
the chosen orthonormal bases. In particular, the same definition applies when
$H_Q=H_L\otimes H_R$, with that residual factor order left unchanged. For an
operator on $(H_G\otimes H_L)\otimes H_R$, use the canonical associator of
the ordered tensor-register construction to view it on
$H_G\otimes(H_L\otimes H_R)$ before taking this partial trace.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

The trace is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]), and the spectral definition makes the expression independent of the eigenbasis. The term for a zero eigenvalue is defined to be $0\ln0:=0$. The default unit is nats, using the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]); the entropy in bits is $S_2(\rho):=S(\rho)/\ln2$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $n\ge1$, let $A_i,B_i:H\to H$ be non-negative for $1\le i\le n$, and let $\lambda_i\ge0$ with $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. Then, in the extended-real order,

$$D\!\left(\sum_i\lambda_iA_i\,\middle\|\,\sum_i\lambda_iB_i\right)\le\sum_i\lambda_iD(A_i\|B_i),$$

where zero-weight terms are omitted from the right side, and the order is that on the extended real line.

Let $V:H\to K$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces satisfying $V^*V=I_H$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative on $H$. Then

$$D(VAV^*\|VBV^*)=D(A\|B).$$

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a
non-negative operator $R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$,
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)$ is non-negative and

$$\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R))=\operatorname{tr}(R).$$

Here $\operatorname{End}(H)$ is the set of linear maps $H\to H$ as in
[[def-qc-partial-trace]], $I_H$ denotes the identity map $x\mapsto x$, and both
conclusions include zero-dimensional factors.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $j:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q$ be the integer embedding of [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], let $\iota_{\mathbb R}:\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R$ be the ordered-field embedding of [[lem-of-q-embeds]], and put $\kappa_{\mathbb R}:=\iota_{\mathbb R}\circ j$. For every integer $m$ and real $\theta$,
$$ (\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^m=\cos(\kappa_{\mathbb R}(m)\theta)+i\sin(\kappa_{\mathbb R}(m)\theta). $$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], [[def-complex-integer-powers]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Define $Xe_j=e_{j+1\bmod d}$ and $Ze_j=\omega^je_j$; these maps are unitary because they respectively permute the basis and multiply its vectors by unit-modulus scalars. If $d\nmid m$, then $q=\omega^m\ne1$, $q^d=1$, and $(1-q)\sum_{b=0}^{d-1}q^b=1-q^d=0$, so $d^{-1}\sum_{b=0}^{d-1}\omega^{bm}=0$; if $d\mid m$, that average is $1$. Choose an orthonormal basis $(u_i)$ of $H_A$ by [F8]. For $0\le r,s<d$, define the linear block $R_{rs}:H_A\to H_A$ by $R_{rs}u_{i^\prime}=\sum_i\langle R(u_{i^\prime}\otimes e_s),u_i\otimes e_r\rangle u_i$, extending linearly. Expanding $R(u_{i^\prime}\otimes e_s)$ in the product basis [F5] then gives $R=\sum_{r,s}R_{rs}\otimes M_{rs}$, where $M_{rs}z:=\langle z,e_s\rangle e_r$: both sides agree on every product basis vector. Direct application to basis vectors gives $Z^bM_{rs}(Z^b)^*=\omega^{b(r-s)}M_{rs}$ and $X^aM_{rs}(X^a)^*=M_{r+a,s+a}$, with indices modulo $d$. For $0\le r,s<d$, $d\mid(r-s)$ exactly when $r=s$, so the proved phase average removes precisely the off-diagonal units. Also $d^{-1}\sum_{a=0}^{d-1}M_{r+a,r+a}=I_B/d$. Therefore $\mathcal T(R):=d^{-2}\sum_{a,b}(I_A\otimes X^aZ^b)R(I_A\otimes X^aZ^b)^*=\sum_rR_{rr}\otimes I_B/d=\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\otimes I_B/d$ by [F3]. When $d=1$, $X=Z=I_B$ and there is only the diagonal unit, so the same formula holds directly.

For non-negative $C,D$ on $H_A$, their tensor products with $I_B/d$ have supports $\operatorname{supp}(C)\otimes H_B$ and $\operatorname{supp}(D)\otimes H_B$ by the tensor-product eigenbases [F7]. Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, fix an ordered
orthonormal basis $\mathcal B$ of $H$, and let
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ be complex-linear. The following are
equivalent: $\Phi$ is completely positive; $J_{\mathcal B}(\Phi)$ is
non-negative; and $\Phi$ has a finite Kraus representation.

Let $H$ and $K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]),
with the root convention that
each inner product is linear in its first argument. Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for
the complex-linear endomorphisms of $H$ and $\mathcal L(H,K)$ for the
complex-linear maps from $H$ to $K$ ([[def-linear-map]]). A **finite Kraus
representation** of a complex-linear map
$\Phi:\mathcal L(H)\to\mathcal L(K)$ is a finite family
$(K_a)_{a\in A}\subseteq\mathcal L(H,K)$ such that

$$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_a X K_a^\dagger\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathcal L(H),$$

where $K_a^\dagger:K\to H$ is the adjoint
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]), which exists
uniquely in finite dimensions ([[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]]).
The composition $K_a\circ X\circ K_a^\dagger$ maps $K$ to $K$, so the sum
defines an output endomorphism for each input endomorphism $X$. The index set
$A$ may be empty; its sum is then the zero map. Zero operators are allowed in
a nonempty family.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let
$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a\in A}K_aXK_a^\dagger$ be a finite Kraus representation,
where each $K_a:H\to K$. The map $\Phi$ is trace-preserving on all of
$\mathcal L(H)$, meaning $\operatorname{tr}_K(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{tr}_H(X)$
for every $X\in\mathcal L(H)$, if and only if
$$\sum_{a\in A}K_a^\dagger K_a=I_H.$$

Let $H_A,H_B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, let $d=\dim H_B\ge1$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative operators on $H_A\otimes H_B$. Then

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_B A\|\operatorname{Tr}_B B)\le D(A\|B).$$

Let $V:H\to K$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces satisfying $V^*V=I_H$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative on $H$. Then

$$D(VAV^*\|VBV^*)=D(A\|B).$$

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For $x,y\in H$, orthonormality and [F3], [F7] give $\langle Vx,Vy\rangle=\sum_j\langle K_jx,K_jy\rangle=\langle x, (\sum_jK_j^*K_j)y\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$; hence $V^*V=I_H$.

Expanding in the environment basis [F8] gives $VXV^*=\sum_{j,k}K_jXK_k^*\otimes M_{jk}$, where $M_{jk}z=\langle z,f_k\rangle f_j$. The partial-trace formula [F6] keeps exactly the terms $j=k$, so $\operatorname{Tr}_E(VXV^*)=\sum_jK_jXK_j^*=\Phi(X)$ for every $X$.

$$D(\Phi(A)\|\Phi(B))\le D(A\|B).$$

The map $\mathcal M_E(X):=\sum_{j<m}\operatorname{tr}(XE_{y_j})\Pi_j$ is a quantum channel from $H$ to $K$. For the indexed register $\mathbb C^\Omega$ with orthonormal basis $|y\rangle$, the unitary identification $Jf_j=|y_j\rangle$ gives the equivalent channel $X\mapsto\sum_{y\in\Omega}\operatorname{tr}(E_yX)|y\rangle\langle y|=J\mathcal M_E(X)J^*$. For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. $$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.
